title: Security essentials
summary: Block open redirects, compare secrets in constant time, keep personal data out of logs, and never build SQL with string formatting.
hints: Redirects: don't write your own check. url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(url, allowed_hosts=allowed_hosts) is already imported and gives True or False. Return url when it's True, and '/' otherwise.

API keys: first if not provided or not expected: return False (this catches both '' and None). Then hmac.compare_digest(provided.encode(), expected.encode()), which takes the same time wherever the keys differ.
Emails: local, at, domain = (email or '').partition('@') always gives three pieces. If any of them is empty, return '***'; otherwise build f'{local[0]}***@{domain}'.

SQL: only change the cursor.execute(...) line. Use a plain string with a bare %s (no quotes around it), and pass the title in a list as the second argument: cursor.execute('SELECT ... WHERE title = %s', [title]).

quiz.question: What's an open redirect?
options: A redirect with no status code
A login page that sends users to any ?next= URL, including an attacker's lookalike site
quiz.explanation: Phishers love them: the link starts with your trusted domain and ends up on theirs. Only redirect to your own hosts.

quiz.question: Why is token == expected risky for secrets?
options: It can return faster the earlier the strings differ, which leaks information through timing
quiz.explanation: A timing attack can guess a secret one character at a time. hmac.compare_digest takes the same time regardless of where they differ.

quiz.question: f"SELECT * FROM task WHERE title = '{title}'": what can go wrong?
options: SQL injection: title = "x' OR '1'='1" changes the query itself
quiz.explanation: Never build SQL with string formatting. Use the ORM, or pass parameters separately so the database treats them as data, not code.
